newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Monday, Feb 24.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Monday, Feb 24.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- SEVEN BILLION STG FRIGATE PROJECT IN DANGER

The Horizon programme, a joint British-French-Italian effort to build Navy frigates, is threated by a dispute over the ship's purpose. France had originally supported the British plan for a multi-purpose "area defence" vessel but, following a cut in the French defence budget, now favours a less sophisticated "point defence" ship. Italy supports the French view.
-- SAFEWAY AIMS TO CUT COSTS BY TRACKING ITS TRUCKS

Supermarket chain Safeway is to spend 1.5 million stg on establishing a satellite tracking system to monitor the movement of its trucks. Computer analysis of the data collected will enable to company to improve its distribution system and save on fuel costs. Logistics director Lawrence Christensen said the company would expect to recoup the cost of the system within a year through increased efficiency.
-- SHELL TO FACE SHAREHOLDER VOTE ON ETHICS

A group of Shell Transport & Trading shareholders want the company to improve its performance on human rights and environmental issues. The group, holding just under one percent of the firm, have tabled a resolution for May's annual meeting. They are worried about such issues as Shell's human rights and environmental record in Nigeria and its plan to sink the disused Brent Spar oil rig at sea, although it has abandoned that under pressure from environmentalists.
-- FEARS OF EMU DELAY LEAD TO BOND INVESTMENT CHANGES

A survey by the US investment bank Lehman Brothers shows international bond fund managers have reduced their exposure to French, Italian and Spanish bonds amid fears that European monetary union could be delayed. There is growing doubt over whether Spain and Italy, in particular, will be able to meet economic convergence criteria in time to join the first round of the single currency.
-- GOVERNMENT NOT HOSTILE TO EMU, INSISTS CLARKE

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke has denied the UK government is hostile to the idea of a single European currency. Speaking on the BBC TV's programme On the Record, Clarke said there was no split in the cabinet over EMU despite comments last week by Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind that the government was "on balance...hostile" to a single currency.
-- LANG SEEKS TO BAN FORMER BARINGS EXECUTIVES

The Department of Trade & Industry has announced it intends to seek court orders disqualifying 10 former Barings bank executives from serving as company directors for 10-to-15 years. Among them is Andrew Tuckey, the bank's former deputy Chairman. Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang intervened following controversy over the Securities and Futures Authority's decision not to take action against either Mr Tuckey or the bank's former chairman, Peter Baring, who is not included in the DTI action.
-- SHETLAND OILFIELD FAILS TO MEET EXPECTATIONS

Several oil companies are expected to scale back plans to develop oilfields in the ocean west of the Shetland Islands. The euphoric reaction to early discoveries in the region has been subdued by problems such as the difficulty of operating in deep water and cold currents. Also, it now appears that natural gas deposits far outstrip oil deposits. Natural gas is much harder to develop and the UK already has a surplus.
-- CLONE SUCCESS RAISES DRUG TRIAL HOPES

Scientists from Edinburgh's Roslin Institute and Scottish biotechnology company PPL Therapeutics have cloned a lamb from the cells of an adult sheep. Ron James, PPL managing director, said that the breakthrough will reduce the time necessary for clinical trials of new drugs. It is also now possible to obtain much greater quantities of certain human proteins available in sheep's milk and used in a variety of medicines.
-- ENERGY TONES DOWN ITS STRATEGY

Energy Group, the demerged former Hanson division, has announced it will scale down acquisition plans in the US following protests from investors. Executive Chairman Derek Bonham said that the company was still looking at acquiring a US energy marketing company, but would be spending tens of millions of dollars rather than the 500 million stg originally envisaged. Investors had expressed concern that Energy Group might pursue a Hanson-style diversification strategy.
-- US TIE UP BY UNITED UTILITIES

United Utilities is seeking an alliance with one of the UK's US-owned regional electricity companies. Many of the US groups that have bought into the UK's electricity industry may prefer to concentrate on distribution rather than competing in the newly liberalised domestic supply market, and United are hoping that a US-controlled group will allow them to take control of that side of the business.
